A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BOTS research. The main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across the substantial appendix reorganization.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix F report original reinforcement-finetuning experiments, hyperparameter ablations, difficulty-estimation results and runtime measurements.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix G report original experiments, including additional reference-model and Dynamic Sampling comparisons. Appendix F.1 also adds a simulation.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 corrects the maximized utility from positive absolute distance to negative absolute distance, aligning the written selection rule with v1's stated goal of selecting near-target tasks. The Bayesian updates, interpolator and Thompson-sampling design remain; the new pseudocode documents these existing components.

E1.justification: V3 adds AMC23 to the 1.5B math evaluations, including Tables 1, 2 and 8. GURU training coverage and the existing math, code and logic benchmarks remain. The retained 7B math evaluation still uses MATH500 and AIME24.

E2.justification: Random, Offline, BOTS-MoPPS and BOTS-DOTS remain in the corresponding comparisons. Appendix G.5 and Figure 11 add an actual evaluation against Dynamic Sampling from Yu et al. (2025) on 1.5B math; v1 discussed oversampling methods without reporting this comparison.

E3.justification: Table 6 retains the main training configurations. New experiments vary reference-model pairs and compare Dynamic Sampling for 55 steps/54.4K tasks with BOTS and Random for 100 steps/25.6K tasks, disclosing approximately 2.5 times greater cost per Dynamic Sampling step. The Offline tie-breaker also changes from Qwen3-8B in v1 Appendix B.6 to 'Qwen3-32B-A3B' in v3 Appendix D.6, conflicting with Section 4.4's retained 30B-A3B description; an actual rerun cannot be inferred.

E4.justification: V1 deferred systematic reference-model ablations to future work. V3 Appendix G.2 tests three reference pairs through both difficulty-prediction quality and downstream training, substantially extending evidence about extrapolation and sensitivity to reference choice. Appendix F.1 adds a noisy, 50-step simulation of the effect of lambda. The posterior-sampling ablation and task-distribution heatmaps are retained.

E5.justification: V3 explicitly reports three-run/seed averages and 95% confidence intervals for central 1.5B math experiments, including Figures 2–3, 7 and 11–14. V1 provides no corresponding run-count or confidence-interval statements. This materially changes uncertainty reporting, without establishing that v1 used only one run; the practice is not extended to all retained experiments.

E6.justification: V3 substantially revises the 1.5B math scores and curves and adds AMC23, reference-choice and Dynamic Sampling results. For example, Table 3's BOTS math TTB(100%) changes from 0.64 to 0.72, but the broader aggregation and newly reported run averaging prevent interpreting this as a like-for-like decline. Tables 4, 7 and 9–13 retain their numerical results.

T1.justification: Appendix F.3 adds Assumption 1 and Proposition 3, with a proof claiming an equivalence between exact interpolation and a task-invariant interpolation coefficient. This is a focused formal addition concerning the existing estimator. Propositions 1–2, their proofs and the exponential-family extensions are retained across relocation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contribution: Bayesian fusion of explicit and implicit evidence, instantiated with lightweight interpolation and Thompson sampling, improves RFT task selection across domains and model scales. The additional experiments support this retained claim.

C2.justification: V3 corrects the main-text explanation of lambda and emphasizes excessive Thompson-sampling exploration at large values. It adds reference-cost amortization, evidence-based reference-choice guidance, the failure case of identical reference success probabilities, and an interpretation of the Dynamic Sampling comparison. Conversely, much of v1 Appendices F.5–F.7's domain-specific interpretation, including qualifications about competitive baselines and converging performance, is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds step-by-step pseudocode and specifies a default Beta(1,1) prior; Appendix D.3 newly identifies verl as the experimental framework. New figures also specify benchmark averaging and smoothing conventions. Existing hardware and Table 6 hyperparameters remain, so these disclosures do not establish a change of implementation.

R1.justification: V3 adds references connecting discounting to Raj and Kalyani, implementation to Sheng et al., and task selection to DATS, model-predictive sampling and SPO. The rewritten background replaces the Ouyang et al. RLHF reference with the GPT-4 report. The central novelty positioning relative to explicit-only and implicit-only selection remains.

P1.justification: V3 creates dedicated hyperparameter and practical-consideration sections, moves proofs earlier in the appendices, adds a pseudocode appendix and rewrites related-work prose. Most per-domain appendix result narratives are removed in favor of displays and captions. Ethics, reproducibility and LLM-use statements are also added, producing substantial structural and explanatory revision.

P2.justification: V3 redraws the main math plots, expands Tables 1, 2 and 8 with AMC23 columns, and adds simulation, reference-choice and Dynamic Sampling displays. Expanded appendix panels show individual benchmarks, confidence bands and separately identified smoothed curves. Many other figures are retained and relocated, but the changed displays constitute a substantial visual revision.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens empirical credibility by adding explicit three-run uncertainty reporting, testing previously unexamined reference choices, and evaluating an external oversampling baseline with computational-cost disclosure. Corrected main-text lambda guidance and pseudocode also improve usability. These gains address important weaknesses in v1 and outweigh localized shortcomings: uncertainty reporting remains concentrated on 1.5B math, some settings are inconsistent, and Proposition 3's necessity argument only establishes agreement outside the chosen batch rather than its claimed global condition.
